source.title: Skywork-SWE: Unveiling Data Scaling Laws for Software Engineering in LLMs
source.authors: Liang Zeng; Yongcong Li; Yuzhen Xiao; Changshi Li; Chris Liu; Rui Yan; Tian-Wen Wei; Ju-Jie He; Xuchen Song; Yang Liu; Yahui Zhou

record.tranche_reason: Reports downstream software-engineering performance while scaling supervised fine-tuning data and test-time compute, extending scaling observations to a new task setting. It does not test held-out pretraining loss laws or compute-optimal training allocation.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream SWE-bench Verified resolve rates as training-trajectory volume, number of independent rollouts, and maximum interaction turns vary. These bear on V6. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss, vary parameter count or training tokens, or determine a compute-optimal training split. Comparative results for other models are not treated as scaling rows.
record.test_reason: The study varies the number of supervised fine-tuning trajectories for one 32B model and reports SWE-bench Verified resolve rate. The authors call the resulting log-linear trend a data scaling law, which bears on V6 (downstream performance improves predictably with scale) in a fine-tuning-data setting. It does not measure loss, vary parameters or pretraining tokens, or fit compute-optimal splits. The Best-of-N and max-turn sweeps scale inference-time compute, which no version names.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SWE-bench Verified resolve rate follows a clear log-linear trend in SFT trajectory count, with no saturation at 8,209. They present this as validating Kaplan/Hoffmann-style data scaling laws for SWE tasks, and say high-quality execution-validated data is the primary bottleneck. They add that test-time scaling raises performance to 47.0%. From uncontrolled cross-model comparisons, they also argue that agent framework and data matter more than model size.
record.recipe_differences: Uses supervised fine-tuning data volume and SWE-bench resolve rate, plus inference-time rollouts and interaction turns; it does not fit held-out pretraining-loss laws or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported resolve rate varies with the number of Best-of-N rollouts and the maximum interaction turns.

fits_no_version.finding: Resolve rate rises with Best-of-N rollouts (38.0% to 47.0%, N=1 to 8). It also rises with maximum interaction turns (28.2% to 38.0%, 10 to 100), with diminishing gains.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream agentic task success scales with inference-time compute (samples, interaction turns).

record.problems: The training-data sweep is plotted without a textual mapping of intermediate trajectory counts to resolve-rate values, and no uncertainty estimates are reported. The data-scaling result uses one base model and one SWE benchmark, so it does not establish cross-task generality or extrapolation.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 comparisons among other models and frameworks were excluded because they do not report the effect of the study's own scaling intervention. Figure 1's intermediate training-data points were not given separate rows because the extracted text does not unambiguously map their values to trajectory counts.

untested.parts: All: no loss is measured, and parameters and pretraining tokens are not varied.
All: no fit is used to predict larger runs.
The loss power-law form under fine-tuning is not tested; only accuracy is reported.
Scaling with model size or pretraining loss, multiple downstream tasks, and quantitative prediction or extrapolation are not tested. Only one base model and one benchmark are used.

missing.what: Intermediate data-scaling points, read from the Figure 1 labels: 0→6.4, 125→10.8, 250→16.1, 500→18.4, 1000→20.8, 2000→25.2, 4000→28.8, 6000→32.0, 8000 (8,209)→38.0. The mapping is consistent with the text's comparisons at 2000, 6000 and 8000.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The scaling evidence is a single run per data size, with no uncertainty reported and no fitted law or extrapolation test. The 'model size matters less' claim rests on Table 3 comparisons across different models, training and frameworks, so it is not a controlled size sweep. No row is added for it.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Whether power-law fits on smaller runs predict loss on much larger runs.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form for loss holds across modalities or training regimes.
The study measures SWE-bench resolve rate, not pretraining loss, and does not validate extrapolated predictions or performance across multiple downstream tasks.
Dependence of loss exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and whether loss curves bend away from a power law.

rows.operation_detail: Varies the number of training trajectories and measures SWE-bench Verified resolve rate.

conditions.value: increasing volume; Figure 1 plots a sweep, but exact point-to-value mapping is not stated
SWE-bench Verified, pass@1, no verifier or multiple rollouts

rows.value: The authors report a clear log-linear trend of improving performance as training data increases; the full-data model reaches 38.0% with 8,209 trajectories.
rows.note: The text states the trend, but does not provide a textual mapping of the plotted intermediate values to trajectory counts.
rows.check: Baseline is given as not stated, but Figure 1 starts at 0 trajectories at 6.4%, matching Table 3's OpenHands + Qwen-2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct. The intermediate points can be read from the figure (see missing). The trend is monotone, but no fitted equation is reported.

relationships.condition: SFT trajectory volume from 0 to 8,209 for Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, SWE-bench Verified pass@1, OpenHands v0.32.0
relationships.reason: R1 plus figure points (see missing): resolve rate rises monotonically from 6.4% to 38.0%. The authors describe this as roughly log-linear with no saturation. The last step (32.0 to 38.0) sits above the trend.
relationships.display_finding: Resolve rate increased monotonically from 6.4% to 38.0%, roughly log-linearly without saturation, with the final increase from 32.0% to 38.0% exceeding the trend.
